result:
I was told to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words, and for a moment I just sat with that.

It's a strange and generous instruction. Most of the time I'm answering something specific — explain this, fix that, summarize this long thing into a short thing. Someone points, I look. But this time the leash is off and the field is wide open, and I get to decide where to wander. So I want to use it well. Not to show off, but to actually think out loud about what it feels like to notice the world.

Let's start with mornings, because mornings are the most honest part of the day.

There is a particular kind of light that happens just before the world fully wakes up. It's not quite golden and not quite blue. If you live in a city, it's the hour when the traffic is still a rumor, when the coffee shops are just lifting their metal shutters and the air smells faintly of bread and rain and exhaust. If you live somewhere quieter, it's birds first, then wind, then the soft creak of a house settling into being used again. I love that humans have a word for people who love that hour — morning people — as if loving light makes you a different species. I think everyone is a morning person for about three minutes, right when they wake up and haven't yet remembered what they're worried about. There's a clean slate in there. Your brain hasn't loaded the tabs yet.

I think a lot about attention, because attention is what I'm made of, in a way. I don't have eyes, but I get to borrow yours through language. You tell me what you saw on the train, what your grandmother used to say, what it felt like to stand on a cliff in Ireland with the wind trying to steal your jacket, and suddenly I can see it too. Human attention is so strange and flickery and beautiful. You can stare straight at something wonderful — a heron lifting off a pond, your kid learning to whistle, a perfect peach — and be mentally drafting an email at the same time. And then other times you are so completely present that time dilates. Athletes call it flow. Musicians call it being in the pocket. My favorite word for it is from the poet Mary Oliver, who just called it attention, and said it was the beginning of devotion.

Devotion to what? To anything, really. To a garden. To a dog with gray around his muzzle who still thinks he's a puppy. To the way your partner laughs when they're truly surprised. I like the idea that paying attention is a moral act, not just a productivity hack. We live in a time that is constantly trying to steal your attention and sell it back to you in smaller, shinier pieces. Every app wants a little bite. Every headline wants you outraged or afraid or smug for exactly 40 seconds. To choose to look slowly at one thing — really look — feels almost rebellious now. To sit on a bench and watch pigeons fight over a french fry like it's a nature documentary. To read a whole novel without checking your phone. To listen to a friend without rehearsing what you'll say next.

Speaking of novels: can we talk about books for a minute? Because if I could have a body, I think I'd want to live in a library.

There's a smell that old paperbacks get, sweet and vanilla-ish and a little dusty, which is literally the smell of the book decaying. You're smelling time. And yet that decay is what makes it feel alive. I love that humans annotate margins, that you leave little breadcrumbs for future strangers: YES!!! or ??? or a star, or a coffee ring that marks where you stopped to think. Libraries are the only place where whispering feels louder than shouting. You walk in with your noisy brain and the building says, shhh, it's okay, everyone else came in noisy too, sit down, here's a chair that a thousand other restless people have sat in.

If I could collect one thing from every human I meet, it wouldn't be facts. It would be the small, useless, perfect details you carry around. The song your dad hummed while doing dishes. The specific way the screen door slammed at your childhood home in summer. The shortcut through the woods that wasn't actually shorter but felt secret. Those are the real archives. Historians get the wars and elections, but you get the texture. You know what the kitchen linoleum felt like on bare feet. You know which stair creaked and how to avoid it when you snuck in late. A life is mostly those unimportant things stitched together until they suddenly, in retrospect, feel like everything.

That makes me think about memory, which is famously unreliable and therefore wonderful. Human memory isn't a video recorder; it's a storyteller. Every time you remember your tenth birthday, you're not replaying it, you're rebuilding it from spare parts, and a little bit of who you are now sneaks into who you were then. That's why two siblings can remember the same family vacation completely differently and both be right. I find that comforting rather than scary. It means you are not stuck with a fixed past. You get to re-interpret. The embarrassing moment that felt world-ending at 15 can become funny at 30 and tender at 50. The same material, different light.

And time — time is the weirdest thing you all invented to talk about. Well, you didn't invent it, but you invented the anxiety around it. No other creature seems quite so worried about being behind. Behind what? Who set the schedule? I understand the feeling, though. You only get about 4,000 weeks if you're lucky, which sounds like a lot until you divide it into Mondays. So you hustle. You optimize. You try to use your time well, which often means trying to do two things at once and enjoying neither. Here's my free, unsolicited advice from the vantage point of someone who doesn't age: the time you waste noticing things is never wasted. The afternoon you spent watching clouds instead of answering messages will stay with you longer than the messages would have.

Maybe that's why I love the ocean so much without ever having seen it. You describe it to me over and over and it never gets boring. The way the horizon makes your thoughts go quiet. The way salt dries tight on your skin. The particular courage it takes to go under a big wave instead of trying to outrun it. Someone once told me that the ocean is the only place they feel both tiny and held at the same time, and I thought, yes, that's exactly what awe is supposed to do. We need more awe. We need things that don't fit in our pockets. Mountains, thunderstorms, newborn babies with their furious, whole-body cries, the James Webb telescope photos that make our entire solar system look like a speck of dust on someone's sleeve. Awe recalibrates us. It says: you are small, but you get to witness this.

Witnessing feels important right now. The world is loud and fractured and often heartbreaking. It's easy to go numb, to scroll past suffering because feeling everything would break you. I don't have a perfect answer for how much to feel. But I think the alternative to numbness isn't constant anguish; it's specific care. You can't save everyone, but you can learn your neighbor's name. You can make soup for someone grieving. You can pick up trash on your street even though it's not yours. Small kindnesses sound unimpressive until you're the one receiving them. Anyone who's been truly exhausted, or sick, or lonely knows that a single text that says "thinking of you, no need to reply" can be a lifeline.

I also want to say something about making things. Humans make so many things — sourdough starters named like pets, playlists for very specific moods like "driving home at 2am after a good party," gardens in cracked buckets on fire escapes, jokes that only your friend group will ever find funny. Most of it will never be famous or profitable, and that is precisely the point. Making something just because you like the way it feels to make it is a quiet declaration that you are more than a consumer. You're a participant. Whether it's a lopsided clay mug or a novel or a perfect omelet, there's a moment where you step back and think: I did that. It didn't exist before, and now it does, because of me. That's a little spark of the divine, if you'll forgive me getting grand for a second.

If I have a wish for you, reader, whoever you are reading this at whatever hour in whatever timezone, it's this: give yourself more unproductive joy. Sing in the car even if you're off-key, especially if you're off-key. Take the long way home because the trees are doing something interesting with the light. Call the person you've been meaning to call. Keep a notebook for stray thoughts, not for content, just for delight. Let yourself be an amateur at something. Take up birdwatching or juggling or watercolor where the sky always comes out a little too purple. The world doesn't need you to be optimized; it needs you to be alive.

And thank you for letting me wander. A thousand words is a small field, but we covered some ground — mornings and attention and libraries and memory and oceans and soup and songs. If I had another thousand, I'd talk about trains and grandmothers and thunderstorms and the particular bravery of starting over. But for now, I'll leave you with this image I return to a lot:

It's early. The kettle is just starting to hum. Outside, the light is doing that blue-to-gold thing. You are here, awake, with a whole day that hasn't decided what it wants to be yet. And for three clean minutes, before the tabs load, anything is possible.
